Unwilling Owner Receives Bank Call Saying Plan Selected – Next Day Bank Says It Was a Mistake

The first deadline of 30 June for Wang Fuk Court owners to submit acceptance-of-acquisition letters to the government has ended. Because more than 75% of owners in Wang Chi House have agreed to sell their titles, the building is being incorporated into the long-term residency scheme. The government says that as of the 16th of this month, it has signed sale-and-purchase agreements with 769 households.

Mr Chan, who lives on a mid-floor unit of Wang Chi House, bought his flat in 2017 and still has about HK$2 million left on his mortgage. He has not signed or returned an 'acceptance-of-acquisition letter'. Speaking to集誌社 last Monday (13th), he said that day he received a call from a staffer at Standard Chartered Bank, which holds his mortgage, telling him the bank had earlier been notified by the government that he had chosen 'Plan B' — the option of taking the money and buying a new Home Ownership Scheme flat.

Mr Chan immediately said he had never signed or returned an acquisition letter and questioned the error, wanting to verify the information. The staffer read out his address, reiterated that it was a government notification, and explained the mortgage arrangements after selling the title, adding that the matter would be recorded and reported to a supervisor.

The following day (14th), Mr Chan received another call from the same staffer, who said that after checking with the bank and reviewing the government-supplied information, it turned out the bank had 'got it wrong'. According to the government's records, he had not selected 'Plan B', and the staffer apologised for the mistake.

Worried about being 'represented' and lacking information, he did not reply

Mr Chan told集誌社 that the reason he has not signed the acquisition letter is that the authorities have yet to answer questions on repair-cost arrangements, insurance compensation, and whether repairs will be carried out to let residents return to Wang Chi House. With too many uncertainties, he cannot decide at this stage to sell his title: 'It's not a case of you say sell and I sell.' He believes the long-term residency scheme is decided only by ballot, and the housing, built with modular integrated construction, is of uneven quality — not attractive enough to make him prioritise selling his flat.

After the earlier announcement that more than 75% of Wang Chi House owners were willing to accept acquisition, Mr Chan already had doubts. He pointed out that many people in neighbourhood chat groups were not selling, and said such figures were merely 'their own claims', with 'no one knowing what goes on in between'. He frankly said, 'If they had voted at the owners' meeting and announced the result straight away, then I'd believe it.' Worried about being 'represented' and having things taken out of context, he has not given any reply.

'No matter what I decide, I'll still have to sell to them'

Regarding the bank's first call, Mr Chan was greatly surprised: 'I never chose anything, yet the government told the bank I'd chosen Plan B.' He gave a wry smile: 'So I'm one of that 75%. I keep telling people I'm not, asking who counts as that 75% — turns out I'm one of them. I've become one without even knowing.'

Mr Chan stressed that the fairest approach would be to vote openly at the owners' meeting and announce the results immediately. However, Hop On (the owners' committee) has stated that the meeting will not deal with the sale of titles, leading him to suspect the authorities are 'afraid that an immediate vote would leave them no room to manoeuvre'. He sighed that this incident made him feel even more that 'no matter how I decide, in the end the government will use its own way to make me sell to them — it's just a matter of whether I sell sooner or later.'

Even the bank's follow-up call the next day saying it had 'got it wrong' has not fully allayed Mr Chan's concerns. 'They say that, I listen to that,' he said.

Even less willing to sell after the owners' meeting

Mr Chan understands the scheme will not change, but still hopes to find out whether there is an option to repair Wang Chi House, which has not yet been demolished, to allow residents to move back. 'Until it's officially announced, we still have a chance that it really can be repaired.' He also pointed out that if the government ultimately legislates to acquire the property, he will have to sell anyway, but if the government does not buy his title, 'you still have to let me go back up and live there.'

At the owners' meeting held on Sunday (19th), Mr Chan questioned whether it was lawful, saying it was merely 'going through the motions' and avoiding residents' questions, 'only talking about whatever it wants to say.' After the meeting, he said he was even more unwilling to sell his title to the government, because repairs to Wang Chi House could be funded by insurance compensation, but once the title is sold, the insurance payout would go to the government.

Housing Bureau: After receiving letters, cases with outstanding mortgages will be referred to banks

集誌社 wrote to the Housing Bureau last Monday (13th) asking whether it was aware of the incident, whether the bureau had erred, whether there had been similar cases and how this affected the earlier published figures, and how residents' trust could be regained. The bureau did not give a direct response, merely replying yesterday (20th) that, according to an announcement in March this year by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the Hong Kong Association of Banks (HKAB), the HKMA, the HKAB and the banking industry will set up a communication platform — including a 'dedicated explanation team' coordinated by the Housing Bureau — to understand the specific needs of Wang Fuk Court residents and provide suitable assistance for each case.

The bureau said it has been in close communication with the HKAB and the banks holding mortgages on Wang Fuk Court units. After receiving a properly signed 'acceptance-of-acquisition letter' from an owner, the explanation team will, based on the mortgage information provided in the letter, refer cases with outstanding mortgages to the lending banks in accordance with the personal-data-collection statement contained in the letter, so that the banks can assign dedicated staff to contact the owners to help them understand the special mortgage arrangements offered by the industry to assist owners, and to provide appropriate assistance.

Standard Chartered: No comment on individual cases, handled with compassion

A Standard Chartered Bank spokesperson replied last Tuesday (14th) that it does not comment on individual client cases. The spokesperson said the bank has had a dedicated team in place to follow up on affected Wang Fuk Court owner-clients on a case-by-case basis with a compassionate approach, and to ensure client data is handled properly.

The first batch deadline for Wang Fuk Court acquisitions ended on 30 June. Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong recently said that as of the 16th of this month, 1,786 households had signed and returned 'acceptance-of-acquisition letters' — more than 90% of all households — of which about 43%, or 769 households, had signed sale-and-purchase agreements.
